reconcile.connective: Defenders read Deuteronomy as an abbreviated restatement that silently presupposes Leviticus' locust exception rather than revoking it.

discrepancy.connective: The source-critical objection is pressed by August Knobel, who argued the Deuteronomist dropped the edible-locust permission because his later age had given up the prohibition's earlier rationale — i.e., D no longer allows what Leviticus does.

skeptic.name: August Wilhelm Knobel
skeptic.work: Die Bücher Numeri, Deuteronomium und Josua (and Die Bücher Exodus und Leviticus)
skeptic.attribution: August W. Knobel (d. 1863), Die Bücher Exodus und Leviticus (1857) and Die Bücher Numeri, Deuteronomium und Josua (1861)

excerpts.excerpt_text: In Deu 14:19 the edible kinds of locusts are passed over, because it was not the intention of Moses to repeat every particular of the earlier laws in these addresses.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly explains the Deut 14:19 vs Lev 11:21-23 tension: Deuteronomy omits (does not prohibit) the permitted locusts because it abbreviates the earlier law; the same note then rebuts Knobel's prohibition reading.
Treats Deut 14:19-20 as cross-referencing the Leviticus list (which includes the edible-locust exception) rather than overriding it, harmonizing the two laws as one body.

pd_work.resource: Keil & Delitzsch, Biblical Commentary on the Old Testament, on Leviticus 11:20 (1861-75)
pd_work.author: Keil & Delitzsch
pd_work.note: K&D treat this passage directly and harmonizingly, explaining the Deut 14:19 omission as abbreviation, not prohibition, and explicitly rebutting Knobel's source-critical reading that D revokes the locust permission.
